problem: How does adding two Int parameters become the returned value 5?
reading: Read one static JVM method invocation. Its local slots keep a=2 and b=3 while iload copies operands onto the stack; iadd replaces them with 5 and ireturn returns that value. These are abstract bytecode operations, not a hardware register diagram.

edges.label: current instruction reads or changes operands

problem: A screen stops collecting locations. Which registration must stop with it?
reading: Follow collection startup to callback registration, then follow location values back to the collector. The cleanup arrow is a separate control relationship: closing or cancelling this collection releases its registered callback through awaitClose.

edges.label: trySend offers values through the channel

problem: A producer outruns its consumer. Will it wait, drop an old value, or retain more work?
reading: Compare four alternative channels under the same attempted sends. They are not connected to each other. Read each queue and producer status together: rendezvous waits for a receiver, capacity two can fill, conflation keeps one latest value, and unlimited buffering consumes memory as the backlog grows.

groups.label: Producer does not wait for buffer space

problem: Job 4 throws. Which siblings are cancelled, and where does supervision stop the spread?
reading: Arrows point from parent jobs to their children. Trace failure upward from Job 4 through ordinary Jobs 2 and 0, then cancellation downward to their other children. The SupervisorJob isolates the other top-level launch; handling the uncaught launch exception is a separate responsibility.

problem: Cancellation reached a suspended load. Can its cleanup still suspend?
reading: The ViewModel controls the load job lifetime. The two cleanup nodes are alternative finally bodies, not two jobs that must both execute. Cancellation unwinds the load; a cancellable suspension can fail during ordinary cleanup, while a short withContext(NonCancellable) block can complete needed suspending cleanup.

problem: Inbox refresh is active but makes no progress. Is it leaked, cancelled, or waiting for a worker?
reading: Use the upper questions to establish ownership, cancellation and error handling. Then connect the dispatcher, suspended location and worker evidence. Those lower arrows are diagnostic relationships: queued parsing depends on an available worker, not on a value moving between question cards.

edges.label: dispatcher determines where queued work waits

problem: Why does changing a cart and assigning a copied state fail to notify StateFlow?
reading: The reference arrows describe the broken variant: the old and copied states share list #1. Mutating that list also changes what the old state sees, so equality-based conflation can suppress the assignment. The final step changes the design to a fresh list; its caption distinguishes the old and new contents.

edges.label: candidate assignment is compared by equals

problem: A set still contains the object in memory. Why can contains(item) return false?
reading: These are illustrative hash buckets in one set, not pipeline stages. Insertion places the item using its original hash. After a hash-relevant property changes, lookup chooses another bucket; the set has not automatically moved the stored entry. Bucket numbers are illustrative rather than a specified HashSet layout.

problem: The tracker property now points to Mixpanel. Why do delegated calls still reach Firebase?
reading: Keep the property and generated delegate field separate. The forwarder calls the delegate captured during construction. Assigning a new tracker changes the public property, not that captured target; the arrow to Mixpanel describes the replacement property value, not a rerouted delegated call.

problem: A property read looks cheap. What work does its delegate actually perform?
reading: Compare three separate delegate contracts. Lazy initialization leads to cached reads; observable performs an assignment before its callback; the custom preference getter performs its own work on each access. No arrow connects one delegate family to another.

edges.label: first successful initialization supplies cached result
getter executes on the calling thread

problem: The object is a Dog but its extension prints the Animal result. Which type selected the call?
reading: Compare two resolution paths for the same declared Animal reference. An overridable member dispatches to the runtime object; the top-level extension is selected using the declared receiver type and compiles to a static JVM function. These paths are alternatives, not successive calls.

problem: Why can adding a library member change which function a recompiled extension call uses?
reading: Follow compile-time resolution. An applicable member wins; only the no-member branch reaches the visible extension. Both branches produce a compiled call, but to different targets. A library update changes this choice when the caller is recompiled, not by dynamically overriding an existing extension.

edges.label: if none applies, consider visible extensions

problem: Where does a slow collector make this unbuffered Flow producer wait?
reading: Follow one value through map and filter to collect. In this sequential pipeline, downstream processing happens before emit returns; there is no implied queue or new coroutine between these operators. The next value starts only after the current downstream work finishes.

groups.label: One sequential collection · no buffer operator

problem: Two counters use the same lambda body. Why do their numbers advance independently?
reading: Each makeCounter invocation creates its own captured count. The arrows connect each returned function to the state it reads and changes; there is no connection between counter a and counter b. The grouping describes closure state, not separate copies of machine code.

edges.label: reads and increments a’s captured count
reads and increments b’s captured count

problem: Why does a negative element skip the rest of the whole function with one return, but only itself with another?
reading: The two groups are alternative implementations. Bare return in this inlined forEach exits process at -1, leaving the remaining suffix unreachable. return@forEach ends only that lambda invocation, so the loop reaches 5 and then Done. Arrows show control progression only where it occurs.

problem: The assignment to List<User> succeeds. Why does reading the first user fail later?
reading: Trace the failing raw-type route from deserialization to element use. The parser received only List, so the unchecked list cast does not establish the element type. The eventual User cast exposes the mismatch. The fix supplies a complete type token or a suitable serializer at the parsing boundary.

edges.label: raw List request lacks User element type
unchecked cast retains the same elements
element use requires a User cast

problem: What remains at this call site after the inline function and lambda are expanded?
reading: The arrows describe compiler expansion, not runtime calls. The function supplies the surrounding Start and End statements; the lambda supplies doWork at the invocation point. Read the emitted statements in order and inspect the final note about the absent function-value boundary in this example.

problem: Which Kotlin declaration choice determines the Java call surface?
reading: Compare four independent Java-facing API shapes. The steps apply the relevant JVM annotation to each declaration. These constructs do not call one another; the point is the member names and available overloads Java callers can actually use.

problem: The Java method returned null. At which Kotlin boundary will that become an error?
reading: The four outgoing arrows are alternative call sites consuming the same unannotated Java result. Explicit non-null assignment and non-null arguments introduce checks; inference can defer failure to a later dereference, while a nullable declaration requires explicit null handling.

problem: A service needs a Tracer. Where does the compiler find that dependency at the call site?
reading: Compare an unsatisfied call with a call inside a scope that provides a Tracer. The requirement comes from submit; its available context can also satisfy validate. The explicit named-argument example is a separate language-feature check in the chapter’s Kotlin 2.4 configuration, not an ordinary value argument.

edges.label: requires a matching context value · missing here
the context value also satisfies validate

problem: A destroyed Activity is still reachable. Which strong-reference chain keeps it alive?
reading: Read each arrow as a strong reference, not a data transfer. The long-lived singleton retains a registered callback, which captures the Activity and therefore its views. Unregistering removes the list-to-callback retention edge; collection is possible only once no other live root can reach these objects.

edges.label: retains callback until it is unregistered

problem: Can a thread see a non-null singleton reference before it sees the writes that initialized the object?
reading: Compare visibility across two threads, not a promised physical instruction order. The unsafe steps illustrate missing publication ordering. With volatile publication, constructor writes before the publishing write become visible after the corresponding volatile read; that ordering is what the labelled edge states.

edges.label: safe variant: initialize before volatile publish
volatile write happens-before subsequent volatile read
then use the safely published fields

problem: An address is absent. Which getters run, and why does the expression still produce a String?
reading: Follow the safe-call dependency chain. The address-null branch bypasses the city getter and supplies the Elvis fallback. The city-to-result edge describes the other branch, where a city value is available; it does not mean the skipped getter executes.

edges.label: read profile if receiver is present
read address if profile is present
read city only if address is non-null

problem: Why does checking a mutable property for null fail to prove a later property read is safe?
reading: Contrast two reads of a changeable property with one captured local value. Another write can intervene between check and use, so the compiler cannot assume the second read matches the first. The local-val alternative supplies one value to both checks and later use.

edges.label: a later property read needs a new guarantee
intervening change can invalidate the earlier check
alternative: check the captured local value

problem: A required JSON name is missing. Will the parser reject it or will a later dereference fail?
reading: Compare the illustrated Gson Unsafe fallback with a configured Kotlin-aware adapter. These are separate parsing routes. The first can bypass constructor checks and leave a null field; the second enforces a required non-null value at the input boundary. Adapter configuration determines the contract.

edges.label: reflection fills only fields present in JSON

problem: Why does nameOf<List<User>>() report List rather than a class that encodes User?
reading: These are separate inline call sites. Each substitutes its own type, but T::class.java asks for a JVM Class, whose identity does not include generic arguments. Compare User, Int and List<User>; choose a richer type representation when nested type arguments matter.

problem: A sealed result gains Cancelled. Which consumers force an explicit decision?
reading: The arrows connect the sealed type to three independent when expressions that consume it. Adding a case invalidates exhaustive expressions without else; a catch-all expression still compiles and can hide the missing domain decision. This is a compile-time dependency map, not a runtime event fan-out.

edges.label: title expression must cover the result cases
icon expression must cover the result cases

problem: Virtual time reached 60 seconds. Why has the task due at that exact instant not run yet?
reading: Separate the test action, virtual clock, scheduled work and recorded attempts. Advancing time excludes tasks at the new endpoint; runCurrent then executes work due at that time. Clock movement is not elapsed wall-clock time, and the diagram makes no benchmark claim.

problem: Where does a Meters value need a wrapper, and why do two collection slots not imply two wrappers?
reading: Compare representation boundaries, not one mandatory execution path. Direct Meters use can keep the underlying value; nullable, generic and supertype uses require boxed representation in the illustrated JVM cases. A generic helper can reuse one already-boxed reference, and later typed use can unbox it. Identity is not the value-class equality contract.

edges.label: generic helper can reuse one boxed reference
typed element use can unbox the value

problem: The binding is val. How can another reader still observe changed collection contents?
reading: Read the arrows as references and operations in the shared-mutable-list variant. val prevents rebinding tags; it does not freeze the target. A read-only List alias sees writes through another mutable alias. The separate final alternative requires an immutable design, not merely a List type or data-class keyword.

groups.label: Mutable target and separate immutable-design alternative

edges.label: fixed binding to the mutable list
read-only alias of the same list

problem: The function returned. What keeps its mutable captured counter alive?
reading: Follow the references from the caller to the returned lambda and its captured mutable cell. The makeCounter stack frame can finish while those heap references remain. Ref.IntRef names the illustrated Kotlin/JVM lowering; this is not a required representation for every backend or optimized compilation.

edges.label: captured var uses a mutable cell in this lowering

problem: Dog is an Animal. Which generic substitutions preserve that safety?
reading: Compare type relationships, not values moving through a system. Starting from Dog <: Animal, an out producer preserves the subtype direction, an in consumer reverses it, and a read/write invariant box permits neither substitution. No edge between the generic alternatives implies inheritance between them.

problem: Why does a Cat write fail at runtime for a Java array, while Kotlin rejects the mutable-list alias earlier?
reading: The Java-array path performs a runtime store check after a covariant alias. The Kotlin nodes are separate alternatives: MutableList is invariant, while read-only List is covariant. Comparing their failure boundaries does not turn the collections into stages of one pipeline.

edges.label: covariant alias permits this compile-time write
array component check rejects incompatible Cat
